# Abstract

Between 1960 and 2025, Polynesia outside Hawai'i and American Samoa more than doubled its resident population while undergoing an extraordinary redistribution across archipelagos, cities and overseas metropolitan diasporas. Across eighteen constant-boundary sub-regions spanning ten modern polities and 63.186,6 km² of buffered coastal and island mask footprint—comprising Samoa, Tonga's five provincial divisions, French Polynesia's five archipelagos, the Cook Islands, Tuvalu, Niue, Tokelau, Wallis and Futuna, Pitcairn Islands and Chilean-administered Rapa Nui—total population rose from 298,4k (298.377) in 1960 to 439,6k in 1980, 554,1k in 2000 and 624,8k (624.787, mean mask density 9,89 inhabitants per km²) by 2025 [@repository1999statistical; @connell2013islands]. Aggregate doubling (+109,4% overall, or +1,14% per annum) conceals a sharp divergence between metropolitan-subsidised or tourism-led growth in the east and remittance-funded emigration plateaus in the centre and west [@bertram1985mirab; @friesen2019beyond]. French Polynesia more than tripled from 79,8k in 1960 to 274,1k on the regional benchmark (278.786 at the 2022 official census), overtaking Samoa as the basin's largest polity after French nuclear-testing investment transformed Tahiti's Windward coast into a 137k metropolitan corridor around Papeete, Faa'a and Punaauia [@ispf2023recensement]. Samoa climbed steadily from 114,4k to 205,6k (+79,6%) and Tonga rose from 64k to 100,2k (+56,6%) despite persistent emigration to New Zealand, Australia and the United States that hollowed out Tonga's outer divisions of Ha'apai and the Niuas [@statistics2022samoa; @department2022tonga; @lolohea2016internal]. By contrast, free-association citizenship and New Zealand labour access triggered steep resident depopulation across Central Polynesia: Niue plunged 67,5% from its 1966 peak of 5.194 (roughly 5,2k) to 1.689 in 2022, the Cook Islands fell from 21.322 in 1971 to 15.040 in 2021, Tokelau drifted from 1.901 in 1966 to 1.647 in 2019 and Pitcairn shrank from 148 to 35 [@niue2023niue; @mfem2022cook; @office20202019; @yamauchi2026when]. Meanwhile, low-lying Tuvalu nearly doubled to 10.632 as Funafuti absorbed over three fifths of its people under mounting sea-level pressure, Wallis and Futuna contracted by a quarter after peaking in 2003 at 14.944, and Rapa Nui quadrupled through mainland Chilean migration and heritage tourism to 7.750 in 2017 before post-pandemic adjustment to 4.800 [@division2018tuvalu; @stsee2024recensement; @milan2015tuvalu]. Across 255 catalogued settlements and 1.768 census observations, urban concentration tightened from a shallow colonial base into a textbook Zipf hierarchy ($\alpha = 1,00$, $R^2 = 0,99$ across the upper 127 settlements) anchored by Greater Papeete, Apia, Greater Nuku'alofa, Rarotonga and Funafuti.

# Background

## Decolonisation, Constitutional Diversity and the MIRAB Economy (1960 to 1985)

At the start of the 1960s, every Polynesian archipelago outside Tonga's British-protected monarchy remained under New Zealand, French, British or Chilean colonial governance. Over the following two decades, decolonisation unfolded along divergent constitutional paths that permanently shaped migration rights, fiscal transfers and census populations [@bertram1985mirab; @connell2013islands]. Western Samoa became the Pacific's first independent sovereign island state on 1 January 1962 under a Treaty of Friendship with New Zealand that guaranteed an annual immigration quota, later dropping the word Western from its official name in 1997 [@statistics2022samoa; @friesen2019beyond]. Tonga ended its British protectorate in June 1970 while retaining uninterrupted royal sovereignty and constitutional land tenure [@department2022tonga]. The Ellice Islands separated peacefully from the Micronesian Gilberts by referendum in 1975 and achieved independence as Tuvalu on 1 October 1978, establishing a new national bureaucracy on the narrow coral rim of Funafuti [@division2018tuvalu; @simati2009effect].

In Central Polynesia, New Zealand negotiated bespoke decolonisation arrangements that preserved full New Zealand citizenship for islanders. The Cook Islands entered self-government in free association in August 1965 and Niue followed in October 1974, whereas Tokelau remained a non-self-governing territory administered from Wellington after referenda in 2006 and 2007 fell short of the threshold for free association [@wrightkoteka2006akau; @niue2023niue; @office20202019; @yamauchi2026when]. France took an opposite integrationist course: following the 1958 referendum, French Polynesia and Wallis and Futuna (formally constituted as an overseas territory in 1961) remained within the French Republic with progressively expanded local autonomy, European-scale civil service salaries and unrestricted citizen mobility toward New Caledonia and metropolitan France [@ispf2023recensement; @stsee2024recensement]. Far to the southeast, Chile granted civil citizenship and lifted movement restrictions on Rapa Nui in 1966 while Pitcairn remained Britain's smallest overseas territory.

These constitutional choices forged what Geoff Bertram and Ray Watters famously diagnosed as the MIRAB economy—driven by Migration, Remittances, Aid and Bureaucracy [@bertram1985mirab]. Because small volcanic islands and coral atolls lacked economies of scale for competitive export manufacturing or bulk agriculture after copra prices slid, Polynesian households allocated kin strategically across urban rim labour markets in Auckland, Wellington, Sydney, Honolulu, Los Angeles and Nouméa [@faanunu2007experiences; @friesen2019beyond]. Remittances from overseas kin funded rural housing, church obligations, school fees and post-cyclone recovery, while overseas aid and metropolitan transfers financed public-sector payrolls in territorial capitals [@lede2015remittances; @connell2013islands]. As a direct consequence, modern Polynesian demography ceased to be a closed biological system of births minus deaths; intercensal change after 1965 depended above all on the balance between high natural increase and constitutional access to overseas migration [@wrightkoteka2006akau; @yamauchi2026when].

## Nuclear-Testing Boom in French Polynesia and Transnational Diaspora Chains

The single sharpest economic and demographic discontinuity in modern Polynesia occurred in Tahiti after Paris selected the Tuamotu atolls of Moruroa and Fangataufa in 1962–1963 as the *Centre d'Expérimentation du Pacifique* (CEP) for French atmospheric and underground nuclear testing [@ispf2023recensement; @connell2013islands]. Between 1963 and 1996, France conducted 193 nuclear tests in the Tuamotus, pouring massive military expenditure, civil engineering contracts, port modernisation and European expatriate personnel into Tahiti. Papeete's newly opened Faa'a international airport (1961) and harbour installations drew thousands of rural Polynesians away from copra and vanilla groves in the Austral, Marquesas, Leeward and Tuamotu archipelagos into wage employment along Tahiti's northwestern coast [@ispf2023recensement]. Windward Islands population nearly doubled in fifteen years from 49.800 in 1962 to 101.392 in 1977, while the suburban commune of Faa'a exploded more than fourfold from 3.681 to 16.950 and Punaauia nearly quadrupled from 2.046 to 7.740. Even after nuclear testing ceased in January 1996, metropolitan fiscal transfers, black-pearl farming in the Tuamotus and high-value resort tourism in Bora Bora, Moorea and Tahiti locked French Polynesia onto a high-income trajectory that prevented mass out-migration [@ispf2023recensement; @repository2003statistical].

Across Western and Central Polynesia, air transport triggered the inverse phenomenon: mass overseas emigration. Opening Rarotonga's international jet airport in 1974 allowed Cook Islanders holding New Zealand passports to relocate rapidly to Auckland factories and service jobs; resident numbers peaked at 21.322 in 1971 and dropped by more than 3.000 within five years, leaving more than four times as many Cook Islanders residing in New Zealand and Australia as on the home islands [@wrightkoteka2006akau; @mfem2022cook]. Niue experienced an even steeper exodus after Hanan International Airport opened in 1971, losing over two thirds of its resident population between 1966 (5.194) and 2011 (1.607), creating one of the highest diaspora-to-homeland ratios on earth [@niue2023niue; @yamauchi2026when]. In Samoa and Tonga, where citizens required visas rather than automatic entry, emigration proceeded through structured family reunification, the Samoan Quota (1.100 places annually), New Zealand's Pacific Access Category (PAC, opened in 2002 for Tonga and Tuvalu) and, from 2007 onward, circular agricultural labour schemes—New Zealand's Recognised Seasonal Employer (RSE) scheme and Australia's Pacific Australia Labour Mobility (PALM) programme [@friesen2019beyond; @simati2009effect; @fatupaito2021samoas; @moalatupou2016social]. By the 2020s, diaspora communities of Samoan, Tongan, Cook Islander, Niuean and Tokelauan heritage across New Zealand, Australia and the United States collectively outnumbered or rivalled every sending homeland [@faanunu2007experiences; @yamauchi2026when].

## Epidemiological Transition, Non-Communicable Disease and Climate Vulnerability (1990 to 2025)

Beneath migration currents, internal vital rates transformed profoundly after 1970. Infant and infectious-disease mortality fell sharply across every archipelago during the 1960s and 1970s through expanded clinics, immunisation and safe water supply, while total fertility declined unevenly—falling near replacement level in French Polynesia and the Cook Islands by the 2010s while remaining elevated near 3,8 to 4,6 children per woman in Samoa and Tonga well into the 2000s [@statistics2010samoa; @repository2003statistical]. Yet life-expectancy gains stalled across parts of Polynesia after 1990 as imported energy-dense diets and sedentary urban lifestyles propelled an epidemic of adult non-communicable diseases (NCDs)—chiefly ischaemic heart disease, stroke and type-2 diabetes [@hufanga2012mortality; @figueroa2021mortality]. In Tonga, careful synthesis of civil registration and health-system records confirms that premature adult male mortality from cardiovascular disease and diabetes kept life expectancy below 68 years across 2010–2018 despite low infant mortality, while cause-of-death audits across Samoa, Tonga, Tuvalu, Niue and the Cook Islands underline how fragile health-information systems remain on small islands [@hufanga2012mortality; @figueroa2021mortality; @l2012mortality].

Simultaneously, twenty-first-century environmental hazards reshaped local settlement geography. Spatial audits across 22 Pacific Island Countries and Territories demonstrate that virtually 100% of residents in Tuvalu, Tokelau, Niue and Tonga's low-lying outer groups, alongside over 90% in Samoa and French Polynesia, reside within 5 km of the coastline—and on coral atolls within a few hundred metres of high tide [@andrew2019coastal]. In Tuvalu, king tides, coastal erosion, saltwater intrusion into *pulaka* taro pits and acute crowding on Funafuti's narrow Fogafale islet (where densities exceed 2.500 per km² of dry land) have provoked both household mobility planning and documented psychological distress [@milan2015tuvalu; @gibson2018relationship]. In Samoa, the catastrophic September 2009 South Pacific tsunami and recurring cyclones (Ofa 1990, Val 1991, Evan 2012) spurred deliberate "climate micro-mobilities"—relocating entire coastal villages inland onto higher volcanic slopes and peri-urban Upolu corridors around Vaitele and Aleisa, buffered financially by counter-cyclical diaspora remittances [@latainiusulu2023climate; @lede2015remittances].

# Methodology

## Eighteen-Sub-Region Admin-1 Partition and Strict Territorial Scope

To capture internal archipelagic redistribution alongside national trajectories from 1960 to 2026, this study partitions Modern Polynesia into eighteen constant-boundary Admin-1 sub-regions grouped across ten sovereign and non-sovereign polities spanning 63.186,6 km² of buffered coastal and island mask area. Hawai'i (US State) and American Samoa (unincorporated US Territory) are strictly excluded so that independent and non-US Polynesian trajectories are not swamped by Honolulu's million-strong metropolitan economy or Pago Pago's US federal transfer regime.

The two largest multi-archipelago polities are disaggregated to first-order administrative divisions. French Polynesia (43.023,1 km² combined mask area) is split into its five official *subdivisions administratives*: Windward Islands (Tahiti and Moorea, 3.437,5 km²), Leeward Islands (Raiatea, Bora Bora, Huahine, Tahaa and Maupiti, 2.962,8 km²), Tuamotu-Gambier (28.160,4 km² across 76 scattered coral atolls and Mangareva), Marquesas Islands (3.475,2 km²) and Austral Islands (4.987,2 km²) [@ispf2023recensement]. The Kingdom of Tonga (5.173 km² combined mask area) is partitioned into its five census divisions: Tongatapu (1.200,4 km²), Vava'u (976,4 km²), Ha'apai (1.938,1 km²), 'Eua (479,7 km²) and Niuas (578,4 km²) [@department2022tonga]. The remaining eight polities enter as single national or territorial units: Samoa (5.254,1 km², covering Upolu, Savai'i, Manono and Apolima), Cook Islands (4.450,7 km²), Tuvalu (1.617,5 km²), Wallis and Futuna (1.083,8 km²), Tokelau (932,6 km²), Niue (649,3 km²), Rapa Nui or Easter Island (611,4 km²) and Pitcairn Islands (390,9 km²).

As in earlier Oceanic cartography, buffered coastal mask areas differ substantially from subaerial land areas. Scattered atolls and small high islands span barely 8,3k km² of true dry land across tens of millions of square kilometres of ocean, whereas coastal mask envelopes aggregate to 63.186,6 km² (almost half of it in Tuamotu-Gambier alone). On the coarse continental raster grid, non-zero pixel sums resolve only the largest western volcanic islands—Samoa (Upolu and Savai'i), Tongatapu and Vava'u—expanding from 158.052 in 1960 to 294.059 in 2025, while the remaining fifteen smaller sub-regions fall below grid pixel resolution and report zero raster totals. All chapter benchmarks therefore derive directly from official census records aggregated across the eighteen Admin-1 sub-regions rather than the coarse continental raster.

## Modern National Census Calendars and Harmonised Benchmark Equations

Every polity in Modern Polynesia maintains regular national or territorial censuses conducted at quinquennial, sexennial or decennial intervals by national statistical offices and metropolitan agencies: the Samoa Bureau of Statistics (1961, 1966, 1971, 1976, 1981, 1986, 1991, 2001, 2006, 2011, 2016 and 2021) [@statistics2022samoa]; Tonga Statistics Department (1956, 1966, 1976, 1986, 1996, 2006, 2011, 2016 and 2021) [@department2022tonga]; ISPF and INSEE in French Polynesia (1962, 1971, 1977, 1983, 1988, 1996, 2002, 2007, 2012, 2017 and 2022) [@ispf2023recensement]; Cook Islands Statistics Office (1961 to 2021 quinquennially, skipping 1991) [@mfem2022cook]; Tuvalu Central Statistics Division (1963, 1968, 1973, 1979, 1985, 1991, 2002, 2012, 2017 and 2022) [@division2018tuvalu]; Statistics Niue (1961 to 2022 across twelve enumerations) [@niue2023niue]; Tokelau National Statistics Office with Stats NZ (fourteen enumerations from 1961 to 2019) [@office20202019]; STSEE and INSEE in Wallis and Futuna (eleven censuses from 1960 to 2023) [@stsee2024recensement]; INE Chile for Comuna Isla de Pascua (1960, 1970, 1982, 1992, 2002, 2012, 2017 and 2024); and annual Pitcairn Islands Government registers (1960 to 2023) [@repository1999statistical; @repository2003statistical].

To align non-synchronous census calendars onto eight standardised regional milestones ($1960, 1970, 1980, 1990, 2000, 2010, 2020, 2025$), each sub-region $j$ interpolates log-linearly between bracketing official census observations $(t_1, P_1)$ and $(t_2, P_2)$:

$$P_j(t) = P_j(t_1) \left(\frac{P_j(t_2)}{P_j(t_1)}\right)^{\frac{t - t_1}{t_2 - t_1}}$$

Where a polity's earliest modern census sits one to three years after 1960 (Samoa, Cook Islands, Niue and Tokelau in 1961; Tuvalu in 1963) or its latest completed census precedes 2025 (2019 in Tokelau; 2021 in Samoa, Tonga and Cook Islands; 2022 in French Polynesia, Tuvalu and Niue; 2023 in Wallis and Futuna and Pitcairn; 2024 on Rapa Nui), the benchmark table holds the nearest official census anchor flat rather than projecting speculative post-census extrapolation. Compound annual growth rates between horizons $t_1$ and $t_2$ follow:

$$g_j(t_1, t_2) = \left(\frac{P_j(t_2)}{P_j(t_1)}\right)^{\frac{1}{t_2 - t_1}} - 1$$

## Settlement Gazetteer Construction and Spatial Scope Stratification

Parallel to Admin-1 totals, the modern gazetteer compiles 255 settlements and 1.768 dated census observations (mean 6,93 observations per site) across all eighteen sub-regions with 0% crowd-sourced fallback. Assembly progressed across four audited source waves: Wave 1 ingested 251 municipal communes, census villages and island administrative towns directly from official national and territorial censuses; Wave 2 added 2 archival island centres from Pacific demographic monographs; Wave 3 reconciled WGS84 coordinates and deduplicated 115 variant orthographies, colonial aliases and contiguous village overlaps within 25 km of canonical entities (such as merging Papeete's colonial variants, Apia's adjoining *Tuamasaga* villages, Nuku'alofa's inner suburbs and Funafuti's individual Fogafale *kainga* quarters into canonical centres); and Wave 4 executed a sub-region gap sweep adding 2 closing settlements (0,79% marginal gain, well below the 2% saturation ceiling), confirming 0 empty sub-regions and 0 unaccounted candidates. Spatial scope strictly distinguishes 4 metropolitan urban envelopes—Papeete (Metro), Nuku'alofa (Metro), Rarotonga (Metro) and Funafuti (Metro)—12 suburban communes or peri-urban towns and 239 city-proper municipalities and island villages, preventing metropolitan aggregates from being double-counted against component communes.

# Testing and Validation

## Cross-Checking Benchmark Totals Against the 108-Row HGIS Panel and Raster Grid

Reconciling the eighteen-sub-region benchmark panel against the independent 108-row Historical GIS (HGIS) administrative table across six modern snapshots (1960, 1980, 2000, 2010, 2020 and 2025, 18 units per regime) confirms tight agreement within roughly one percentage point at every horizon (detailed in Appendix Table \ref{tab:hgis-regimes}). At 1960, the HGIS panel totals 296.547 against our chapter benchmark of 298.377 (−0,61% offset), the narrow 1,8k gap arising because the HGIS Samoa unit back-interpolates to 1960 (110.782) whereas the chapter benchmark holds Samoa's official 1961 census anchor (114.427), partially offset by higher HGIS French Polynesia coverage (81.635 versus 79.820).

From 1980 through 2025, HGIS totals sit slightly above chapter benchmarks by +0,48% (1980: 441.749 versus 439.636), +1,07% (2000: 560.072 versus 554.145), +1,02% (2010: 603.896 versus 597.809), +0,8% (2020: 628.705 versus 623.701) and +0,76% (2025: 629.516 versus 624.787). Every single person of the closing 4.729 discrepancy in 2025 traces transparently to a single sub-region: Tuamotu-Gambier. While the official 2022 ISPF census enumerated 278.786 across French Polynesia—including 16.729 across the 76 Tuamotu atolls and Gambier—our simplified Tuamotu-Gambier submask series anchors on a conservative 12.000 figure (omitting 4.729 remote-atoll and garrison-era fluctuations), leaving the other seventeen sub-regions matching HGIS and official national census publications to exact single-person precision [@ispf2023recensement; @statistics2022samoa; @department2022tonga]. Meanwhile, checking the three raster-resolved high-island sub-regions (Samoa, Tongatapu and Vava'u) against their combined benchmark sums confirms exact 0% parity across every quinquennium from 1970 (207.164) through 2025 (294.059), verifying spatial raster alignment on high volcanic islands.

## De Facto Versus De Jure Enumeration, Disaster Spikes and Census Drift

Modern Polynesian census series are statistically dense, yet four methodological features require careful scrutiny before drawing demographic conclusions [@l2012mortality; @office20202019; @department2022tonga]. First, Polynesian micro-states oscillate between *de facto* (present on census night) and *de jure* (usual resident) enumeration rules. On tiny atolls such as Tokelau, a single inter-island ferry sailing or church conference can shift headcounts by 5% to 8%; Tokelau's 2019 population count recorded 1.647 residents (up from 1.383 in 2013) partly because usual-resident definitions and returning diaspora visits expanded census-night coverage [@office20202019]. Similarly, Cook Islands totals reflect substantial seasonal tourist turnover on Rarotonga and Aitutaki unless non-resident visitors are carefully filtered from resident tables [@mfem2022cook].

Second, external geopolitical and economic shocks generate abrupt single-island spikes that stand out vividly in census records. On Tureia in the southern Tuamotus, official ISPF counts leapt from 1.478 in 1977 to 2.934 in 1983 and 2.186 in 1988—reflecting French military and technical personnel stationed at nearby Moruroa and Fangataufa nuclear test sites—before plunging to 313 in 2002 and 261 in 2022 once testing ended [@ispf2023recensement]. On Rapa Nui, INE Chile censuses recorded soaring growth from 3.765 in 2002 to 7.750 in 2017 fuelled by mainland Chilean hospitality workers and tourism booms, followed by a sharp post-pandemic contraction to 4.800 in 2024 after extended COVID-19 air-link closures and stricter residency controls restricted non-Rapanui stays. Third, volcanic and tsunami disasters trigger localised relocations: Tonga's January 2022 Hunga Tonga-Hunga Ha'apai eruption occurred immediately after the November 2021 census (100.179) and displaced coastal villages on Tongatapu, 'Eua and Ha'apai, just as the 2009 tsunami accelerated inland migration in Samoa [@latainiusulu2023climate; @department2022tonga].

# Results

## Regional Trajectory: Rapid Post-Independence Expansion to Emigration Plateau (1960 to 2025)

Modern Polynesia's 65-year demographic curve traces a classic decelerating logistic ascent, shown in Figure \ref{fig:poly-trajectory}. From 298,4k inhabitants in 1960, aggregate population surged by +2,53% per annum across the opening decade to 383,2k in 1970 as high post-war fertility collided with plummeting infant mortality and the onset of French Polynesia's nuclear-testing construction boom [@repository1999statistical; @ispf2023recensement]. Thereafter, expanding overseas migration channels and gradual fertility decline bent the regional curve steadily flatter: growth slowed to +1,29% per annum across 1970–1990 (439,6k in 1980 and 495,4k in 1990), +0,94% per annum across 1990–2010 (554,1k in 2000 and 597,8k in 2010) and just +0,29% per annum across 2010–2025 (623,7k in 2020 and 624,8k in 2025) [@repository2003statistical; @connell2013islands]. Across the closing five-year window from 2020 to 2025, net regional expansion virtually stalled (+0,03% per annum) as falling fertility in French Polynesia, emigration losses across Tonga, Cook Islands and Wallis and Futuna, and post-pandemic contraction on Rapa Nui nearly offset modest natural increase in Samoa.

<figure class="crd-figure-block" id="fig:poly-trajectory">
<img class="crd-figure-img" src="/artefacts/project_austral/1.0-modern-polynesia/modern_polynesia_population_trajectory.png" alt="fig:poly-trajectory" loading="lazy" />
<figcaption class="crd-caption"><span class="crd-caption-label">Figure 2.</span> Modern Polynesian demographic trajectory from 1960 to 2025 across leading sub-regions (Panel A) and top ten sub-regional mask density rankings in 2025 (Panel B).</figcaption>
</figure>

Behind that smooth aggregate deceleration lay a historic eastward swing in regional demographic primacy—exacting a reversal of the colonial century's westward shift. In 1960, Samoa led Polynesia with 114,4k inhabitants (38,3% of the regional total), well ahead of French Polynesia (79,8k, 26,8%) and Tonga (64k, 21,4%). By the mid-1990s, Tahiti's Windward Islands alone had caught up with Samoa; by 2025, French Polynesia commanded 43,9% of Modern Polynesia (274,1k benchmark; 278,8k official 2022 census), while Samoa's share eased to 32,9% (205,6k) and Tonga's fell to 16% (100,2k) [@ispf2023recensement; @statistics2022samoa; @department2022tonga]. Together, those three polities accounted for 92,8% of the region's population in 2025 (up from 86,5% in 1960), while the seven smaller polities combined shrank from 13,5% to 7,2% of regional residents. Table \ref{tab:polity-shares} summarises these ten-polity structural shifts, and Table \ref{tab:census-series} lists official national and territorial census returns across six modern census waves from 1960–1966 to 2019–2024.

## French Polynesia: Nuclear-Era Boom and Tahiti's Metropolitan Dominance

French Polynesia's demographic transformation after 1962 stands without parallel in the South Pacific. Growing +243,3% on our harmonised benchmark from 79,8k in 1960 (84.551 at the 1962 census) to 274,1k in 2025 (278.786 at the 2022 ISPF census), the French overseas collectivity accounted for nearly three fifths of Modern Polynesia's entire 65-year population increase [@ispf2023recensement; @repository2003statistical]. Yet expansion was intensely lopsided across its five archipelagos.

The Windward Islands (Tahiti and Moorea, mask area 3.437,5 km²) quadrupled from 47k in 1960 (49.800 in 1962) to 84.552 in 1971, 123.069 in 1983, 162.686 in 1996, 184.224 in 2002 and 209.980 in 2022—raising their territorial share from 58,9% to 75,3% and achieving a mask density of 61,09 inhabitants per km², second only to Tongatapu [@ispf2023recensement]. Inside Tahiti, urban expansion spilled rapidly beyond historic central Papeete, whose municipal population peaked at 26.926 in 2017 (26.654 in 2022), into a dense coastal metropolitan ring spanning Faa'a (soaring from 3.681 in 1962 to 29.826 in 2022), Punaauia (2.046 to 28.781), Mahina (6.524 in 1977 to 14.623), Pirae (3.948 to 14.068), Paea (5.619 to 12.756) and Arue (5.911 to 10.322). Together, the *Unité Urbaine de Papeete* expanded from 77.781 in 1977 to 137.030 in 2022—nearly half of all French Polynesia—while outer-Tahiti commuter communes such as Papara (11.743), Afaahiti on the Taiarapu isthmus (6.829), Papeari (5.446) and Mataiea (5.391), alongside Moorea's coastal districts of Paopao (4.895), Haapiti (4.109) and Afareaitu (4.055), absorbed secondary spillover [@ispf2023recensement; @andrew2019coastal].

Outer French Polynesian archipelagos experienced more measured yet sustained recovery after decades of colonial stagnation. The Leeward Islands more than doubled from 16.177 in 1962 to 36.007 in 2022, propelled by luxury resort tourism on Bora Bora—where Nunue grew from 1.590 in 1977 to 5.541 in 2022 and Faanui jumped from 472 in 1962 to 3.312—alongside Raiatea's administrative port Uturoa (3.663) and Avera (3.440) [@ispf2023recensement]. The Marquesas Islands doubled from 4.838 in 1962 to 9.478 in 2022 across Taiohae on Nuku Hiva (2.218), Atuona on Hiva Oa (1.993) and Hakahau on Ua Pou (1.654), finally restoring a modest fraction of their pre-colonial vitality. The Austral Islands expanded gently from 4.371 in 1962 to a 2017 peak of 6.965 before edging down to 6.592 in 2022 across Moerai on Rurutu (987) and Mataura on Tubuai (929), while Tuamotu-Gambier swung sharply with nuclear-era garrisons (Tureia peaking at 2.934 in 1983) and black-pearl aquaculture (Rangiroa rising from 949 in 1977 to 2.785 in 2022; Makemo and Takaroa expanding through the 1990s before pearling downturns).

## Western Polynesian Emigration States: Samoa, Tonga and Wallis and Futuna

In Western Polynesia, persistently high natural increase fought a running battle against sustained overseas migration to New Zealand, Australia, the United States and New Caledonia [@friesen2019beyond; @faanunu2007experiences; @fatupaito2021samoas].

Independent Samoa (5.254,1 km² mask area; 2.682 km² subaerial HGIS area) added more than 91k residents across six decades, climbing from 114.427 at the 1961 pre-independence census to 146.647 in 1971, 156.349 in 1981, 161.298 in 1991, 176.710 in 2001, 187.820 in 2011 and 205.557 in 2021 (mask density 39,12 per km²; subaerial density 76,6 per km²) [@statistics2022samoa]. Growth was punctuated by two sharp emigration waves during the 1970s–1980s (when annual growth dipped to just 0,14% across 1981–1986) and again after the expansion of RSE and PALM seasonal labour programmes in the late 2010s, yet Samoan total fertility remained high enough to maintain continuous positive net expansion [@statistics2010samoa; @fatupaito2021samoas]. Spatially, Samoa underwent pronounced suburbanisation along Upolu's northwest corridor: while historic Apia city proper peaked at 38.836 in 2001 and eased slightly to 35.974 by 2021, peri-urban satellites west of the capital boomed—Vaitele climbing from 5.200 in 2001 to 8.224 in 2021, Faleasiu reaching 4.431 and upland Aleisa Sasa'e surging eightfold from 470 in 2001 to 3.810 in 2021 as households sought freehold land and inland safety after cyclones and the 2009 tsunami [@statistics2022samoa; @latainiusulu2023climate; @lede2015remittances]. Meanwhile, Savai'i stagnated near 43k to 45k residents around its ferry gateway Salelologa (1.850 in 2021).

The Kingdom of Tonga (5.173 km² mask area) climbed rapidly from 64k in 1960 (77.429 at its 1966 census) to 90.085 in 1976, 94.649 in 1986 and 101.991 in 2006, before hitting a prolonged emigration plateau at 103.252 in 2011, 100.651 in 2016 and 100.179 in 2021 [@department2022tonga; @hufanga2012mortality]. Beneath national stagnation, internal migration concentrated Tongans relentlessly onto the main island of Tongatapu (detailed in Appendix Table \ref{tab:tonga-divisions}) [@lolohea2016internal]. Tongatapu doubled from 37,1k in 1960 (47.920 in 1966) to 75.416 in 2011 and 74.320 in 2021 (74,2% of the kingdom; mask density 61,91 per km², highest in Modern Polynesia), anchored by Greater Nuku'alofa (peaking at 36.045 in 2011, 34.142 in 2021; core city 21.185) and expanding southern villages Vainī (3.295) and Ha'ateiho (2.627) [@department2022tonga]. Raised-limestone 'Eua grew swiftly through 1966–2006 (5.206) after resettling volcanic Niuafo'ou evacuees before easing to 4.864 in 2021, and northern Vava'u around Neiafu (3.825) hovered near 14,2k. By contrast, Ha'apai suffered relentless depopulation—plunging 58,1% from 13.533 in 1966 to 5.665 in 2021 as households left Lifuka for Nuku'alofa, Auckland and seasonal work abroad—while the remote Niuas halved from 2.368 in 1986 to 1.148 in 2021 [@lolohea2016internal; @moalatupou2016social; @figueroa2021mortality].

Wallis and Futuna (1.083,8 km² mask area) traced a distinctive rise-and-fall arc tied to New Caledonia's nickel economy. Resident population rose from 8.313 in 1960 to a historic maximum of 14.944 in 2003 as return migration and public infrastructure spending briefly retained youth, before collapsing 25,4% over two decades to 13.445 in 2008, 12.197 in 2013, 11.558 in 2018 and 11.151 in 2023 (density 10,29 per km²) [@stsee2024recensement]. Every major village on Uvea and Futuna shrank in tandem—territorial capital Mata-Utu sliding from 1.940 in 1962 to 980 in 2023 and Leava on Sigave dropping from 480 in 2003 to 302—leaving more Wallisians and Futunans in New Caledonia (over 22k) than on their home islands [@stsee2024recensement].

## Free-Association Depopulation and Climate-Exposed Micro-Polities

Across Central Polynesia's New Zealand realm, unrestricted citizenship generated the sharpest sustained peacetime resident declines in modern Oceania [@bertram1985mirab; @wrightkoteka2006akau; @yamauchi2026when]. Niue (649,3 km² mask area) provides the archetype: from 4.864 in 1961 and a post-war peak of 5.194 in 1966 (roughly 5,2k), rapid air-linked emigration to Auckland slashed numbers to 3.281 in 1981, 2.239 in 1991, 1.788 in 2001 and a floor of 1.607 in 2011, before modest return migration and tourism stabilised residents at 1.784 in 2017 and 1.689 in 2022 (density 2,6 per km²), with over a third clustered in Alofi (606) while outer villages like Namukulu (9 in 2022) shrank to handfuls of households [@niue2023niue]. The Cook Islands (4.450,7 km²) climbed from 18.378 in 1961 to a peak of 21.322 in 1971 prior to airport opening, then fell sharply to 17.614 in 1986, hovered near 17,4k to 19,3k through 1996–2016 as Rarotonga's tourism economy drew Fijian and Filipino hospitality workers, and dropped to 15.040 in 2021 during pandemic border closures [@wrightkoteka2006akau; @mfem2022cook]. Internal centralisation intensified dramatically: Rarotonga grew from 8.676 (47,2% of the nation) in 1961 to 10.863 (72,2%) in 2021 around Avarua (5.113) and Arorangi (2.661), while southern and northern outer islands such as Mangaia, Atiu, Penrhyn and Manihiki lost over half their post-war residents [@mfem2022cook]. Tokelau (932,6 km²) declined gently from 1.901 in 1966 to 1.383 in 2013 before recovering to 1.647 in 2019 across Atafu (541), Fakaofo (506) and Nukunonu (452), supported by New Zealand budgetary transfers and a diaspora exceeding 8k in New Zealand [@office20202019; @yamauchi2026when].

Low-lying Tuvalu (1.617,5 km² mask area; barely 26 km² of true coral dry land across nine atolls) followed a contrasting trajectory of near-doubling coupled with extreme atoll urbanisation [@division2018tuvalu; @milan2015tuvalu]. National population nearly doubled from 5.444 in 1963 to 7.349 in 1979, 8.750 in 1991, 9.359 in 2002 and 10.632 in 2022 despite PAC emigration to New Zealand and maritime seafarer remittances [@simati2009effect; @division2018tuvalu]. Virtually every bit of that growth piled onto the capital atoll of Funafuti, which multiplied nearly tenfold from 687 residents (12,6% of Tuvalu) in 1963 to 2.120 at independence in 1979, 3.962 in 2002 and 6.602 in 2022 (62,1% of the nation), pushing Fogafale islet past extreme urban crowding while outer islands such as Nanumea (Lolua falling from 1.051 in 1963 to 229 in 2022) and Niutao (Kulia down from 797 to 345) emptied steadily [@division2018tuvalu; @milan2015tuvalu; @gibson2018relationship].

On Polynesia's southeastern rim, two remote micro-polities diverged completely. Rapa Nui (611,4 km² mask area) recorded the highest proportional expansion of any territory in the region (+322,9% across 1960–2025): lifting Chilean movement restrictions and launching LAN-Chile air links in 1967 multiplied Hanga Roa's population nearly sevenfold from 1.135 in 1960 to 1.936 in 1982, 3.765 in 2002, 5.761 in 2012 and 7.750 in 2017 as archaeological tourism boomed, before pandemic closures and residency law enforcement trimmed the 2024 census back to 4.800. Neighbouring Pitcairn Islands (390,9 km²) traced relentless terminal attrition, sliding 76,4% from 148 inhabitants in 1960 to 55 in 1982, 44 in 2001 and just 35 residents in Adamstown by 2023—the smallest permanently inhabited jurisdiction in Oceania [@connell2013islands].

## Modern Urbanisation and Zipf Consolidation

Over the 65 years after 1960, Modern Polynesia's urban hierarchy transformed from a flat, polycentric colonial shelf into a remarkably disciplined Zipf distribution, illustrated in Figure \ref{fig:poly-hierarchy}. Upper-half rank-size regression across the top 127 of 255 catalogued settlements yields a near-unit Zipf exponent of $\alpha = 1,00$ ($R^2 = 0,99$; full 255-centre slope $-1,27$, $R^2 = 0,89$). Excluding the twelve suburban communes—preventing Papeete's metropolitan suburbs from inflating the upper mid-tier—retains an exceptionally crisp power-law fit of $\alpha = 0,91$ ($R^2 = 0,98$ across the top 121 centres; full 243-centre slope $-1,18$, $R^2 = 0,87$).

<figure class="crd-figure-block" id="fig:poly-hierarchy">
<img class="crd-figure-img" src="/artefacts/project_austral/1.0-modern-polynesia/modern_polynesia_urban_hierarchy.png" alt="fig:poly-hierarchy" loading="lazy" />
<figcaption class="crd-caption"><span class="crd-caption-label">Figure 3.</span> Twelve largest catalogued modern Polynesian settlements (Panel A) and rank-size distribution across 255 centres with upper-half power-law fit ($\alpha = 1,00$, $R^2 = 0,99$ across the top 127 centres, Panel B), 1960 to 2025.</figcaption>
</figure>

Five metropolitan and national urban anchors now dominate regional settlement geography: Greater Papeete (137k in 2022), Apia city proper (38,8k peak in 2001; 36k in 2021, flanked by rapidly growing Northwest Upolu suburbs Vaitele at 8,2k and Vailele at 3,6k), Greater Nuku'alofa (36k peak in 2011; 34,1k in 2021), Rarotonga Metro (11,5k peak in 1971; 10,9k in 2021) and Funafuti Metro (6,6k in 2022), alongside booming Rapa Nui centre Hanga Roa (7,8k peak in 2017) [@ispf2023recensement; @statistics2022samoa; @department2022tonga; @mfem2022cook; @division2018tuvalu]. Combined, those five capital urban agglomerations hold roughly 224,6k residents at latest census—36% of Modern Polynesia's entire resident population, rising past 40% once contiguous peri-urban Upolu and Tongatapu commuter rings are included [@andrew2019coastal; @connell2013islands]. Urban concentration has thus become the defining spatial counterpart to transnational emigration: while overseas capitals absorb Polynesian youth across the Pacific Rim, domestic capitals drain their own outer archipelagos.

# Limitations

Four structural limitations qualify this modern demographic synthesis. First, buffered coastal mask areas (63.186,6 km²) systematically understate real-world crowding on habitable coral islets and narrow volcanic coastal strips [@andrew2019coastal]. Tuvalu's mask density reads 6,57 inhabitants per km² across 1.617,5 km² of buffered reef footprint, yet actual subaerial land density exceeds 409 per km² nationally and surpasses 2.500 per km² on Funafuti's Fogafale islet; similarly, Tokelau's 1,77 per km² mask density conceals true atoll densities above 135 per km² on barely 12 km² of dry coral [@division2018tuvalu; @office20202019]. Coarse continental raster validation likewise remains limited to Samoa, Tongatapu and Vava'u because the other fifteen sub-regions fall below pixel thresholds.

Second, a known 4.729 headcount gap separates our Tuamotu-Gambier submask series (12.000 in 2025) from the official 2022 ISPF census total for Tuamotu-Gambier (16.729), accounting for 100% of the +0,76% offset between the 2025 HGIS total (629.516) and the chapter benchmark (624.787). Because Tuamotu-Gambier encompasses 76 scattered atolls including former military test sites at Moruroa and Hao, simplified two-anchor submask interpolation smooths out the sharp 1977–1996 CEP garrison bulge and post-1996 pearling cycle [@ispf2023recensement]. In addition, buffered submask polygons assign three southern Tuamotu-Gambier settlements (Tureia, Gambier and Hereheretue) to the adjacent Austral Islands mask boundary rather than Tuamotu-Gambier, a minor spatial edge effect documented explicitly in the companion gazetteer.

Third, resident census totals capture only the island-based half of contemporary Polynesian populations [@yamauchi2026when; @friesen2019beyond]. Because Cook Islanders, Niueans and Tokelauans hold New Zealand citizenship, Wallisians and Futunans hold French citizenship, and large Samoan and Tongan diasporas reside permanently in Auckland, Sydney, Utah, California and Hawai'i, island-only census curves measure territorial residency rather than ethnic demographic survival. Fourth, non-synchronous census calendars (2019 in Tokelau through 2024 on Rapa Nui) mean that our 2025 closing benchmark holds recent pre-2025 official counts flat, leaving post-2021 disruptions—above all Tonga's January 2022 Hunga Tonga-Hunga Ha'apai tsunami displacement and post-COVID PALM/RSE labour departures from Samoa and Tonga—to be quantified in the 2026 census round [@fatupaito2021samoas; @department2022tonga; @l2012mortality].

# Conclusion

Between 1960 and 2025, Modern Polynesia outside Hawai'i and American Samoa doubled its resident population from 298,4k to 624,8k while reorganising its political, economic and spatial geography from top to bottom [@connell2013islands; @bertram1985mirab]. Growth slowed monotonically across every decade—from +2,53% per annum in the 1960s to +0,03% per annum in 2020–2025—as MIRAB labour migration, fertility transition and rising NCD adult mortality reshaped island vital balances [@hufanga2012mortality; @figueroa2021mortality; @friesen2019beyond].

Rather than moving in lockstep, the ten polities fractured into three clear demographic regimes. French Polynesia surged by +243,3% under French nuclear-era investment, metropolitan transfers and tourism to overtake Samoa as the basin's largest polity (43,9% share), building a 137k metropolitan agglomeration along Tahiti's Windward shore [@ispf2023recensement]. Western Polynesia's sovereign states—Samoa (205,6k) and Tonga (100,2k)—balanced high natural increase against heavy transnational emigration and intense internal centralisation onto Northwest Upolu and Tongatapu, while Wallis and Futuna contracted by a quarter after 2003 [@statistics2022samoa; @department2022tonga; @lolohea2016internal; @stsee2024recensement]. Finally, Central Polynesia's free-association micro-states—Niue (−67,5% from its 1966 peak), the Cook Islands (−29,5% from 1971) and Tokelau—shifted the majority of their peoples permanently overseas, even as low-lying Tuvalu doubled into extreme Funafuti atoll crowding under acute climate-vulnerability pressure and Rapa Nui quadrupled via tourism [@niue2023niue; @mfem2022cook; @milan2015tuvalu; @gibson2018relationship]. Together, these forces tightened Polynesia's 255-centre urban hierarchy to a crisp Zipf law ($\alpha = 1,00$, $R^2 = 0,99$), defining an oceanic world at once more urban, more transnational and more environmentally exposed than at any point in its history [@andrew2019coastal; @latainiusulu2023climate].

# Footnotes

All numerical values follow European decimal commas, full-stop thousands separators and semantic magnitude abbreviations (k for thousands). Constant-boundary Admin-1 tables cover eighteen sub-regions across ten polities from 1960 to 2025 and strictly exclude Hawai'i and American Samoa. Buffered coastal mask areas (63.186,6 km²) encompass archipelagic envelopes exceeding dry subaerial land area; coarse continental raster sums resolve only Samoa, Tongatapu and Vava'u, while full regional totals reconcile directly against official national and territorial censuses and the 108-row Historical GIS panel.
